title: A Tutorial On Attentiveness; Plus Thoughts On The Power Of Review
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Written as the school year winds down, Linsin responds to a wave of teacher emails about students losing focus and links to five previously published strategies for improving attentiveness: getting students to listen, speaking with power instead of repeating directions, a following-directions strategy, using the word 'go' effectively, and giving unforgettable directions. He then pivots into a reflection on the value of reviewing strategies after trying them, drawing an analogy to a jiu-jitsu video course where the real understanding comes only after attempting a move and revisiting the instructions. He argues the same is true for classroom management: rereading a strategy after using it deepens understanding until it becomes second nature rather than a memorized technique.
points: Even the final days of the school year are valuable teaching time and shouldn't be sacrificed to post-testing malaise or 'senioritis.'
The article compiles five previously published attentiveness strategies as a refresher for keeping students focused through the end of the year.
Real mastery of a classroom management strategy comes not from reading it once but from trying it out and then reviewing it again afterward.
Reviewing a strategy after attempting it in the classroom is when it moves from mere technique to becoming part of a teacher's natural approach.
Linsin draws a personal analogy to learning jiu-jitsu, noting the biggest leap in understanding comes after physically trying the move, not from watching alone.
quotes: Even a day left of school is an opportunity for learning—an opportunity effective teachers will want to squeeze to the last drop.

To let things go, to let behavior and attentiveness spiral south, to pitch away the last vestiges of a living, working, and vibrant classroom would be a crime—punishable by regret, disappointment, and a summer waiting on redemption.

Reading through a strategy a couple times, taking notes, and visualizing yourself using it in your classroom before putting it into action is smart and a sure way to avoid disaster. But the real learning, the real deepening of a strategy and its nuances, takes place after trying it out.

It’s during your review of the strategy—the quiet moments sitting alone at your desk or computer, reading through the strategy once again while replaying your performance in your head—when the light bulb really begins to brighten.

The review is when the written instructions begin making “a-ha” sense, when the strategy becomes absorbed into your consciousness . . . Making it not just a mere strategy. But part of who you are and the way you teach.
